issues.legal_issue: A government cannot cancel all dealership selections merely because allegations of improper selection have arisen in some cases, without assessing the allegations, the selections, and the effects of blanket cancellation.
material_facts: The selection boards had published merit panels for thousands of locations, and allotments included both operational dealerships and applicants awaiting further formalities.
Media reports alleged political patronage in a subset of selections; the government cancelled all selections without examining any individual case, even on a preliminary basis.
The government had not assessed whether the allegations had substance, whether the selections were generally tainted, or the impact of cancellation on the different categories of selectees.
The selection process was governed by detailed guidelines, and a mechanism existed for considering complaints against selections.
issues.conclusion: The blanket cancellation order was arbitrary and violated Article 14; it was quashed except in respect of cases referred for independent examination.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 prohibits arbitrary state action and treating unequals as equals. State decisions must be based on fair play and application of mind. In Common Cause, A Registered Society v. Union of India (1996) 6 SCC 530, the Court required transparent and objective procedures for such allotments; Mahabir Auto Stores v. Indian Oil Corporation (1990) 3 SCC 752 and Kumari Shrilekha Vidyarthi v. State of U.P. (1991) 1 SCC 212 support review of arbitrary public action, including in a contractual setting. The mass-cancellation decisions in Bihar School Examination Board v. Subhas Chandra Sinha (1970) 1 SCC 648 and B. Ramanjini v. State of A.P. (2002) 5 SCC 533 were distinguishable because they involved evidence of widespread wrongdoing, unlike the unexamined allegations here. A blanket cancellation may be permissible where a large number of selections are prima facie tainted and separating tainted from untainted selections is difficult, but the mere existence of controversy is insufficient.

rule.if: challenge_to_blanket_selection_cancellation and government_cancelled_all_selections and allegations_limited_to_some_selections and no_individual_assessment and (selection_process_had_complaint_mechanism or selectees_included_distinct_categories)

predicates.challenge_to_blanket_selection_cancellat: Applicants challenged a government order cancelling selections for public-sector dealerships and distributorships.
predicates.government_cancelled_all_selections: The government cancelled all selections made through the selection process.
predicates.allegations_limited_to_some_selections: Allegations of improper selection concerned only a subset of the selections.
predicates.no_individual_assessment: The government did not examine individual selections or assess the allegations even preliminarily before cancelling them all.
predicates.selection_process_had_complaint_mechanis: The selection guidelines provided a mechanism for considering complaints about selections.
predicates.selectees_included_distinct_categories: The selected applicants included different categories of people whose circumstances and eligibility bases differed.

issues.definition: When a blanket cancellation of public selections is challenged, limited allegations combined with no individual assessment make the blanket cancellation invalid, even where a complaint mechanism or distinct groups of selectees exist.

issues.legal_issue: Selections specifically alleged to have resulted from political patronage or other extraneous considerations require independent examination rather than resolution through cancellation of all selections.
material_facts: Media reports identified particular allotments alleged to involve political connections or patronage.
The government had not examined those cases, even preliminarily, before cancelling every selection.
The Court made no finding that the identified selections were in fact tainted and considered independent examination necessary to determine whether they were based on merit.
The Court noted that the public has a right to know the circumstances in which elected representatives obtained such allotments.
issues.conclusion: The Court appointed an independent committee to examine the identified cases and directed that the challenged order remain applicable to those cases pending the committee's report and further orders.
issues.legal_principle: Common Cause, A Registered Society v. Union of India (1996) 6 SCC 530 treats public allotments as requiring fair and just administration and recognizes the duty to scrutinize allotments made for political favour or to influence decision-makers. Allegations of such favouritism call for examination on their merits; they do not justify treating all selectees alike or avoiding scrutiny through blanket cancellation.

predicates.challenge_to_cancellation_of_public_deal: Applicants challenged a government order cancelling selections for public-sector dealerships and distributorships.
predicates.specific_allotments_alleged_to_be_politi: Particular allotments were alleged to have resulted from political connections, patronage, or other extraneous considerations.
predicates.no_independent_examination_of_allegation: No independent body had examined whether the identified allotments were based on merit or extraneous considerations.

issues.definition: When specific public allotments are alleged to have been politically influenced and no independent examination has occurred, independent review is ordered while the challenge to their cancellation is considered.

issues.legal_issue: Writ review is available to challenge arbitrary government action affecting dealership selections and agreements, even where the affected parties have contractual arrangements with public-sector oil companies.
material_facts: Some selectees had entered into agreements with oil companies, some had received letters of intent, and others had been placed on published merit panels.
The government cancelled the selections as a policy decision, not because the affected applicants had breached contractual terms or failed to meet selection requirements.
The government argued that contractual terms and the availability of other remedies made writ proceedings inappropriate.
issues.conclusion: The objection that writ proceedings were an inappropriate remedy was rejected; the government action could be reviewed for arbitrariness and violation of Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 review applies to arbitrary public action even where the relationship also has a contractual dimension. Mahabir Auto Stores v. Indian Oil Corporation (1990) 3 SCC 752 holds that public action by a state-controlled corporation may be challenged on public-law grounds such as arbitrariness and requires fair and reasonable treatment; the availability of contractual remedies does not by itself bar such review.

predicates.writ_challenge_to_government_action_affe: Applicants brought writ proceedings challenging government action affecting their dealership selections or related arrangements.
predicates.government_action_not_based_on_contractu: The government cancelled the selections for a policy reason rather than because the applicants breached their agreements or failed selection requirements.
predicates.public_authority_exercised_state_power: A government authority exercised public power in taking the challenged action.

issues.definition: When a public authority uses state power to affect dealership selections for a reason other than contractual breach, writ review is available despite the contractual relationship.
